en: The *Carmavastu* (80v6 = GBM 6.742; MSV IV 159). Summary verse (*uddāna*):
Ordination by means of the five, bedding and seating, and so forth. [The remainder of the verse follows].
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

At that time, in a village called Vāsava near the city of Aśmaka, there lived a householder named Balasena, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa; he had taken a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her;
yet as he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself, neither a son nor a daughter was born to him.
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods.

He supplicated the deity of the grove, the deity of the forest, the deity of the crossroads, the deity who accepts offerings, the innate deity, the co-religious deity, and even the deity who is constantly attached to him.
Furthermore, there is this common worldly saying that sons and daughters are born as a result of supplication;
however, that is not so.
If it were so, each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
However, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three?
When the mother and father are in love and have come together,
when the mother is healthy and in her fertile period, and when a gandharva is present—
if these three conditions coincide, sons and daughters are born.
While he remained thus intent on his petition,

there was a certain being in his final existence, seeking [the goal], having grasped the path to liberation, turned inward toward nirvāṇa and turned away from saṃsāra, having no desire for any rebirth or death among all states of existence, and bearing his final body.
Having passed away from one of the classes of gods, he descended into the womb of that Prajāpatī. There are five unique qualities found in certain women of wise nature.
What are these five?
He knows a man who is impassioned; he knows one who is dispassionate;
he knows the time; he knows the season.
He knows when the embryo has entered the womb;
he knows from whom the embryo enters;
and he knows whether it is a male child.
He knows whether it is a girl:
if it is a boy, he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a girl, she remains resting against the left side of the womb.
Delighted and overjoyed, she informed her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, may you prosper! I have become pregnant with a living being. Since it remains resting against my right side, it will certainly be a boy."
He too, filled with joy, uttered this inspired exclamation:
"May I indeed behold the face of a son long desired; may he be born equal to me and not inferior;
may he perform his duties for me, support me when I am aged, and inherit my estate; may my family lineage endure for a long time."
"And when we have passed away, having given gifts, whether small or great, and having performed meritorious deeds, he will dedicate the merit in our names, saying:
'May this follow those two wherever they go, whatever state of rebirth they have attained.'"

Knowing that she had conceived, he attended to her while she was staying on the upper terrace of the palace, providing her with whatever she desired; in cold weather with cold provisions and in heat with warm provisions, and with food prescribed by physicians that was neither too bitter,
nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent— being free from the qualities of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.
Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces; like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat without descending to the ground below,
and she heard nothing unpleasant until the full maturation of the fetus.
After the passing of eight or nine months,

she gave birth; a boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, golden-hued, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad and expansive forehead, joined eyebrows, a prominent nose, and [adorned] with an inlay of jewels.
Adorned with a fastened central gemstone,
the householder Balasena summoned jewel appraisers and said to them,
"Sirs, determine the value of these jewels."
"It is not possible to determine the price of these jewels.
Now, it is the natural law that for whatever jewel it is impossible to set a price, a "ten-million" (koṭi) is assigned as its value.
They said: [This is the case.]
“Householder, the value of these jewels is ten million.
His kinsmen, having gathered and assembled together, performed an extensive birth ceremony for the newborn for three weeks— twenty-one days— and established his name.
"What shall be the name of this boy?
the kinsmen asked.
They said, "This boy was born under the asterism Śravaṇā, while wearing an earring set with jewels worth ten million."
"Let the boy's name be Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa.
On the very day that Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa was born, two servant boys were born to the householder Balasena;
he established the name of one as Dāsaka and the other as Pālaka.

Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to play with him, two to cleanse him, and two to suckle him. Raised by these eight nurses, he grew rapidly on milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other most excellent, refined nourishments, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, calculation, finger-calculation, sealing, subtraction, depositing, and the examination of building sites and the examination of gems.
He became an opener of seals, an expounder, a scholar, and one of quick action in these eight examinations.
His father then had three dwelling-houses constructed for him.
He had three pleasure gardens laid out: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season. He also established three harems:
the senior, the middle, and the junior.
He, having gone up to the palace roof, played, took pleasure, and amused himself with musical instruments performed by men.
Meanwhile, the householder Balasena was constantly engaged in his agricultural work.
Koṭīkarṇa saw that father.
He was constantly engaged in agricultural work.
[The son] asked him,
"Father, for what purpose are you always so intent on agricultural work?"

He said, "Son, if I too were to play, enjoy, and amuse myself just as you do, seated upon the roof-terrace of the palace with instrumental music performed by men, our wealth would before long be diminished."
They would go to complete exhaustion and total depletion.
He reflected:
"This exhortation is being directed at me alone."
He said,
"Father, if that is so, I shall take my merchandise and go to another country.
His father said:
"My son, I possess such a vast quantity of jewels that even if you were to consume them according to the analogy of sesame seeds, rice, jujubes, and horse-gram,
there would still be no depletion of my jewels.
He said:
"Father, give me leave; I am going to another country taking my merchandise.
Balasena, knowing his persistence to be absolute, granted him permission.
Then Balasena, the householder, had a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell in the village of Vāsava: "Who among you is able [to travel] with Śroṇa..."

"Let him gather merchandise suitable for the great ocean so that he may embark upon the great ocean together with the caravan leader Koṭīkarṇa, free from customs duties and without having to pay a toll.
Five hundred merchants gathered merchandise suitable for the great ocean.
The householder named Balasena reflected:
"By what kind of vehicle will Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa go? He then reflected further.
If the elephants are delicate and difficult to maintain,
and the horses also are delicate and difficult to maintain,
then the donkeys are mindful and delicate.
"Let him go by means of a donkey-cart.
He was summoned by his father and told:
"Son, you must not go ahead of the caravan, nor should you go behind it."

"If the thief is strong, he will fall upon the caravan from the front; if he is weak, he will fall upon it from the rear. You must travel in the middle of the caravan, lest the caravan leader be killed and the caravan be destroyed. He also addressed Dāsaka and Pālaka: [The text continues: "If the thief is strong, he will fall upon the caravan from the front; if he is weak, he will fall upon it from the rear. You two must travel at the sides of the caravan, lest the caravan leader be killed and the caravan be destroyed. They both agreed, saying, "So be it. Then the caravan leader said to the merchants, "Friends, you must travel with great care and vigilance. Having said this, he departed. Then the thief, having observed that the caravan was traveling slowly, approached from the front. Seeing him, the caravan leader said to the merchants, "Friends, this thief is powerful; he has come from the front. All of you must exert yourselves with great effort. At that time, the merchant named Dāsaka was positioned at the very front of the caravan. When the thief saw Dāsaka, he thought, "This man is strong and capable; I cannot overcome him. He then turned back and fled. The merchant Dāsaka pursued him for some distance, but when he could not overtake him, he returned. The caravan leader asked, "Dāsaka, did you see the thief? He replied, "I saw him, but I could not overtake him. The caravan leader said, "Friends, this thief is extremely swift; we cannot catch him. We must proceed with even greater speed. The merchant named Pālaka was positioned at the rear of the caravan. When the thief saw Pālaka, he thought, "This man is weak and incapable; I can easily overcome him. He then turned back and attacked. The merchant Pālaka fought with him for some time, but when he could not overcome him, he returned. The caravan leader asked, "Pālaka, did you see the thief? He replied, "I saw him, but I could not overtake him. The caravan leader said, "Friends, this thief is extremely swift; we cannot catch him. We must proceed with even greater speed. At that time, there was a certain monk who had been practicing meditation in the forest. He heard the sound of the caravan's departure and thought, "The caravan is traveling slowly; they will surely be harmed by robbers. I should go and inform them. He went to the caravan leader and said, "Caravan leader, why is your caravan traveling so slowly? You will surely be harmed by robbers. The caravan leader replied, "Venerable sir, do not speak thus. This thief is extremely swift; we cannot catch him. The monk said, "Caravan leader, I am a forest-dwelling monk. I have seen many such thieves before. I shall go ahead and wait for you. Having said this, he went forward and waited. Then the thief, seeing the monk, thought, "This man is a forest-dweller; he will not be able to help me. He then proceeded to attack the caravan. At that moment, the monk, seeing the thief attacking, thought, "Alas! These merchants are being destroyed. I must save them. He then transformed himself into a great bull and stood blocking the path. The thief, seeing the bull, thought, "This bull is strong and capable; I cannot overcome him. He then turned back and fled. The bull pursued him for some distance, but when he could not overtake him, he returned. The caravan leader asked, "Venerable sir, did you see the thief? He replied, "I saw him, but I could not overtake him. The caravan leader said, "Venerable sir, this thief is extremely swift; we cannot catch him. The monk said, "Caravan leader, I am a forest-dweller. I have seen many such thieves before. I shall go ahead and wait for you once more. Having said this, he went forward and waited again. Then the thief, seeing the monk, thought, "This man is a forest-dweller; he will not be able to help me. He then proceeded to attack the caravan. At that moment, the monk, seeing the thief attacking, thought, "Alas! These merchants are being destroyed. I must save them. He then transformed himself into a great lion and stood blocking the path. The thief, seeing the lion, thought, "This lion is fierce and powerful; I cannot overcome him. He then turned back and fled. The lion pursued him for some distance, but when he could not overtake him, he returned. The caravan leader asked, "Venerable sir, did you see the thief? He replied, "I saw him, but I could not overtake him. The caravan leader said, "Venerable sir, this thief is extremely swift; we cannot catch him.
