"My two sons, Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa must not be released by you under any circumstances.
Then, at another time, Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa—having performed the auspicious rites for success and well-being—approached his mother, prostrated at her feet, and said:
"Mother, I am going; look upon me with favor, for I am setting out for the great ocean."
She began to weep.
He said,
"Mother, why do you weep?"
His mother, her face clouded with tears, said,
"Son, shall I ever see my little son alive again?
He reflected:
"I have set out with auspicious rites,
yet she utters such an inauspicious word.
Enraged, he said:
"Mother, having performed the auspicious rites for success and the recitation of blessings, I have set out for the great ocean.
If you continue to perform such inauspicious acts,
do you not see the states of woe?"
She said,
"Son, you have uttered harsh words of speech;
confess your transgression as a transgression."
"Perhaps this karma may thus reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total termination.
She then asked for forgiveness for her transgression.
Then Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, having performed the auspicious rites of protection and well-being, set out with carts, loads, baskets, and boxes.
Having loaded a vast quantity of merchandise for transport by sea onto camels, oxen, and donkeys, he set out for the great ocean.
Traveling by stages through villages, towns, market towns, hamlets, and cities, he eventually reached the shore of the great ocean.
Having carefully prepared a sea-going vessel, that carrier of wealth set out upon the great ocean. Driven by a favorable wind, he reached the Island of Jewels.
Having examined them repeatedly, he filled that ship with jewels until it was like a vessel full of sesame, rice, jujubes, and horse-gram.
With his vessel successfully completed, he reached Jambudvīpa, driven by a favorable wind.
That caravan encamped right there on the seashore.
Then that merchant leader Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, taking Dāsaka and Pālaka with him, withdrew from the midst of the caravan to a secluded spot and began to calculate income and expenditure.
Afterwards, he said to Dāsaka:
"Dāsaka, go and see what the caravan is doing. He went and saw that they were all asleep together.
He too fell asleep right there.
Thinking that Dāsaka was taking a long time, Pālaka was addressed:
"Pālaka, go see what the caravan is doing."
He went on until he saw a caravan being harassed by a wild ox; he,
too, began to harass the caravan with the wild ox.
Dāsaka reflected:
"Pālaka will summon the caravan leader.
Pālaka also reflected: [the same].
"Dāsaka will call for the caravan leader.
That caravan, having made its camp for the night, set out while it was still dark;
he too lay down, overcome by a deep sleep.
The caravan proceeded until dawn;
they then asked,
"Sirs, where is the caravan leader?"
He goes ahead;
having gone ahead, they ask, "Where is the caravan leader?
He comes from behind.
Going behind, they ask, "Where is the caravan leader?
When he goes into the middle,
they go into the middle and ask.
When even there he was not found,
Dāsaka said,
"The thought occurred to me that Pālaka will summon the caravan leader."
Pālaka also said,
"The thought occurred to me that Dāsaka would summon the caravan leader.
Gentlemen, you have not done well in that we abandoned the caravan leader."
"Come, let us turn back.
They replied, "Sirs, if we were to turn back, we would all meet with disaster through this improper course."
"Come, let us first make an agreement:
until the merchandise has been unloaded, no one must inform Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa’s parents. Having made this agreement, they departed.
The parents of Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa heard that Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa had arrived; they went out to meet him and asked,
"Where is the caravan leader?"
He comes to the middle;
having gone to the middle, they ask, "Where is the caravan leader?
They reply:
He came from behind;
having gone behind, he asked,
"Where is the caravan leader?"
"He is going ahead! they said, and they were thus thrown into confusion until their goods had been secured.
Once he had departed, they spoke among themselves.
"Mother, we forgot about the caravan leader.
One of them returned and said,
"This Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa has arrived."
Having given him those two as a welcoming gift, they went out to meet him but did not see him;
then another person came and said,
"This Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa has arrived."

Having given him that escort, the two set out to meet him but did not see him; they did not begin to believe in anyone else until they wrote letters, along with umbrellas, bells, and fans, in the gardens and temples, saying: "If Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa is still alive, may he return quickly."
Then, having passed away and died from that place of rebirth, he was destined for a superior state of existence.
The two of them, weeping out of grief, became blind.
At the time of sunrise, he too was awakened by the rays of the sun, yet when he looked, he did not see his caravan.
Otherwise, those two would remain as donkeys. Having yoked them, he set out;
however, on a sandy plain, the path was blocked by the wind.
The mindful donkeys, having sniffed [the path], set out and proceeded slowly; yet when touched by the goad-stick, they entered the Śālā forest.
Afflicted by thirst and with distressed faces, they went along with their tongues lolling out.
Seeing them, compassion arose within him.
He reflected:
"If I do not release them, I shall meet with disaster through these very men.
Having released them, he set out on foot.
He saw an iron city, high and lofty;
at its gate stood a man who was dark, fierce, and wrathful, with blood-red eyes, his body bound with a mass of flesh, and holding an iron club in his hand.
He approached him and said,
"O man,
is there any water here?"
He remained silent.
When questioned by him once more as to whether there was water there,
he again remained silent.
Having entered there, that caravan leader uttered the cry, "Water! Water!

At that moment, Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa was surrounded by about five thousand hungry ghosts who resembled scorched pillars, stood like skeletons, were covered with their own hair and body hair, had bellies like mountains, and mouths like the eye of a needle.
They said, "O caravan leader, you are compassionate; please give us, who are afflicted by thirst, some water.
He replied:
"Sirs, I too am searching for water; from where could I give you water? They replied, "Caravan leader, this is a city of hungry ghosts (preta); how indeed could there be water here?"
"Today, for twelve years, we have heard the sound 'water, water' from you.
He replied:
"Who are you, sirs, and by what karma have you been reborn here?
They replied, "Śroṇa, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful; they will not believe you."
And he said: "Sirs, I am an eyewitness; why should I not have faith?"
They recite this verse:
"We were revilers and wrathful; we were miserly and stingy. Even a tiny gift was not given by us, and because of that, we have come to the world of hungry ghosts."
"Śroṇa, go! You are one of great merit and power.
Have you ever seen anyone who, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts, emerged alive with safety and well-being?"
Having entered the city, he went on living. As he set out,
he eventually saw that man.
He was told by him:
"O gentle-faced one, had it been made known to you that this was a city of hungry ghosts (preta-nagara), alas, I would not have entered here.
He was thus addressed by him.

"Śroṇa, go! You are one of great merit and power, since you have entered the city of the hungry ghosts and emerged in safety and well-being. Having set out, he saw another city made of iron, high and towering.
There too, at the gate, stood a man who was Time—fierce, red-eyed, with a protruding belly, and holding an iron club in his hand.
He approached him;
having approached, he spoke thus:
"O man, is there water here in this city?
He remained silent. Being questioned by him once more, he [remained silent].
"O man, there is water here in this city.
He remained silent.
Then, having entered there, he made the sound "Water! Water! (pānīyaṃ pānīyam).
He was surrounded by many thousands of hungry ghosts (*preta*), who resembled burnt pillars,
stood upright like skeletons of bone, were covered with their own hair and body hair, possessed bellies as large as mountains, and had mouths like the eye of a needle. They said:
“Śroṇa, you are compassionate; please give us water, for we are tormented by thirst.
He replied, “Sirs, I myself am searching for water; how could I give you water?”
They said, "Śroṇa, this is a city of hungry ghosts; how could there be water here?
For twelve years now, we have heard the sound 'water, water' coming from your direction."
He asked, "Who are you, sirs, and by what karma have you been reborn here?
They replied:
"Śroṇa, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful; they will not believe you.
He replied, "Sirs, I am one who has seen it with my own eyes; why should I not believe?"
They recite this verse:
"Intoxicated by the pride of health, intoxicated by the pride of youth and wealth,
we did not give even the slightest gift, because of which we have come to the world of hungry ghosts."
"Śroṇa, go! You are one of meritorious deeds.
Has anyone ever been seen or heard of by you who, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts (preta), emerged alive, safe, and sound?
He then set out.
When he saw that man,
he said to him:
"O gentle-faced one, oh, if you had informed me that this was a city of hungry ghosts (preta), I certainly would not have entered here."
He said, "Śroṇa, go; you are one of great merit and power.
Have you ever seen or heard of anyone who, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts, emerged alive, safe and sound?"
Having set out, he saw that at the time of sunset there was a celestial mansion, and four apsarases who were beautiful,

graceful, and lovely to behold; and a man, handsome, lovely, and graceful, adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments, who was sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying with them.
He was seen by them from afar;
they began to address him:
"Welcome, Śroṇa! Are you not thirsty or hungry?"
He reflected:
"Surely this must be a god, or a nāga, or a yakṣa. And he said:
"Noble one, I am thirsty; I am hungry. He was bathed and fed by them, and he remained in that celestial palace until the time for the rising of the sun.
He was told by them, "Śroṇa, descend; there will be danger here.
Having descended, he stepped aside and stood at a distance.
Thereafter, at the time of the sun’s rising, that celestial mansion vanished;
those celestial nymphs also vanished, and four brindled black dogs appeared.
Having cast that man face down, they tore out his vertebrae one by one and devoured them until the time of the sun’s setting.
Thereafter, that celestial mansion appeared once more, and those apsarases appeared as well.
That man—handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments—played, took delight, and enjoyed himself together with them.
He approached them and said:
"Who are you, and by what karma have you been reborn here?
They replied, "Śroṇa, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful; they will not believe you."
He said, "I am an eyewitness; how could I not believe it?
Śroṇa, I was once a sheep-butcher in the village of Vāsavagrāmaka."
"Having slaughtered sheep again and again, and having sold their meat again and again, I make my living.
But the noble Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion for me, comes and says:
'Worthy sir, the ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable.'"
"Desist from this evil, unrighteous act!
But I did not desist at his word;
he exhorted me again and again.
"O gentle-faced one, the ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable.
Desist from this evil, unrighteous dharma!
Even then, I did not desist.
(83v = GBM 6.749) He asked me: "O gentle-faced one, do you slaughter these sheep during the day or at night? I replied:
"Noble sir, I shall kill you by day. He replied, "Good sir, why do you not undertake the observance of the precepts at night?"
From him, I received the undertaking of the precepts at night.

Because of the ripening of that karma of having undertaken the precepts at night, I experience such divine happiness precisely during the night. Because of the ripening of that karma of having slaughtered sheep during the day, I experience such suffering precisely during the day.
And he spoke this verse:
"By day I was a tormentor of the lives of others, but by night I was endowed with the virtues of moral conduct;
it is the fruit of that very action—both auspicious and sinful—that I now experience."
"Śroṇa, will you go to Vāsavagrāma? "I will go;
my son lives there."
He makes his living by slaughtering sheep again and again.
You should say to him: "I have seen your father. He will then say:
"The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this evil, unrighteous act!
O man, as for what you say—that the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful—"
He will not believe it.
Śroṇa, if he does not believe, you should say: "Your father says that beneath the slaughtering block, a jar full of gold has been placed."
"Having extracted that [debt], satisfy yourself with perfect happiness; provide for the noble Mahākātyāyana with alms from time to time, and dedicate the merit in our names.
In this way, perhaps this karma may become thin, exhausted, and brought to an end.
He then set out.
At the time of sunrise, he saw another celestial mansion;
there was a single apsaras, beautiful, lovely,

and pleasing, and a single man, also handsome, lovely, and pleasing, adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments, who was sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying with her.
Seeing him from afar, he began to address him:
"Welcome, Śroṇa! Are you not thirsty? Are you not hungry?
He reflected:
"Surely this must be a god, or a nāga, or a yakṣa," he thought.
He said,
"I am thirsty and I am hungry."
He was bathed and fed by them;
he remained in that celestial palace until the time of the sun's setting. Then he was addressed by those two:
"Śroṇa, descend; there will be a danger here.
Having seen the danger, he descended and stood to one side.
Then, afterwards, at the time of the sun's setting...
At the time of the sun’s descent, that celestial palace vanished;
that apsaras also vanished,
and a great centipede appeared.
Having wound her body around that man’s body seven times, she devoured his head until the very time of the sun’s rising.
Thereafter, that celestial mansion appeared once more,
and that apsaras also appeared.
And that man was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments, he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
He approached him and asked:
"Who are you, and by what karma have you been reborn here?"
He spoke thus:
"Śroṇa, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful; they will not believe you.
He replied:
"I am one who has seen it with my own eyes; why should I not believe it?
He replied, "In the village of Vāsava, I was a brahmin who committed adultery."
And the noble Mahākātyāyana, having come out of compassion for me, said:
"O gentle-faced one, the ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this evil, unrighteous dharma.
Yet, by his word, I did not desist.
Again and again he dissuaded me, saying:
"O worthy one, the ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable;
desist from this evil, unrighteous dharma!"
Nevertheless, I did not desist from that evil and unwholesome practice.
He asked me:
"O gentle-faced one, do you go to another's wife by day, or rather at night?"
I said to him,
"Noble sir, it is night.
He replied:
"O gentle-faced one, why do you not take up the observance of the precepts during the day?
"I have taken up the observance of the precepts during the day from him.
"Because of the ripening of that karma—namely, the observance of the precepts during the day which I took up from the noble Mahākātyāyana—I experience such divine happiness during the day."
"Because of the ripening of that karma—having approached another's wife at night—I experience such suffering as this during the very night.
And he spoke this verse:
"Deluded by another's wife at night, yet endowed with the virtues of moral conduct during the day."
Indeed, I am now experiencing the fruit of that karma, whether auspicious or evil.
"Śroṇa, you will go to Vāsavagrāmaka.
There is a brahmin there who is my son and an adulterer; he should be told this:"
"I have seen your father;
he says, 'The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this evil, unrighteous practice.
And he said:"
"O man, you say,
'The people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful,' yet no one will believe you."
"Śroṇa, if he does not believe you, you should say: 'Underneath the Agniṣṭoma fire-pit, your father filled a golden jar and buried it.
Take that out and satisfy yourself with perfect happiness; and from time to time provide alms-food for the noble Mahākātyāyana, and in our names dedicate the merit of this offering.
By this, perhaps this karma may become thin, exhausted, and brought to an end.'"
Having set out,
he saw another celestial mansion.
Therein was a woman, beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold, adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments.
In its four legs, which were like the feet of a couch, four hungry ghosts were bound and standing;
seeing him from afar, she began to address him:
"Śroṇa, welcome! Do not [fear]."
"Are you thirsty, or are you hungry?
He reflected:
"Surely she must be a goddess, or a nāga maiden, or a yakṣī."
He said, "Noble lady, I am thirsty; I am hungry.
She bathed him, fed him, and spoke to him.

"Śroṇa, if they search for anything, do not give it to them," she said, and desiring to make those beings witness the karma they themselves had performed, she entered the celestial palace and remained there.
They began to search, saying, "Śroṇa, you are compassionate; we are hungry, so give us something."
When one was thrown [a morsel], a floating husk appeared;
when another was thrown, he began to eat an iron ball;
when another was thrown, he began to eat his own flesh.
When another person spat, pus and blood appeared;
he saw that it had come out with a foul odor.
"Śroṇa, you were forbidden by me; why did you give this to them? he asked.
"What use have you for compassion? You yourself are more compassionate.
He said, "Sister, who are these people of yours?"
She said:
"This is my husband; this is my son."
"This is my daughter-in-law;
this is my slave girl. He said:
"Who are you, and by what karma have you been reborn here?
She replied, "Śroṇa, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful; they will not believe you."
"Sister, I am one who has seen it with my own eyes;
why would I not believe it?
She replied:
I was a brahmin woman in the village of Vāsavagrāmaka.
When the night of the constellations had arrived, I prepared and set out a choice meal.
And the noble Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion for me, entered Vāsavagrāmaka for alms.
I saw him, with a body inspiring confidence and a mind inspiring confidence.
Seeing that his mind was serene, I, having conceived a sense of devotion, offered him almsfood. Then the thought occurred to me: "I shall rejoice in my husband; he will experience great joy."
When he had bathed and returned, I said to him, "Noble son, rejoice that the noble Mahākātyāyana has been provided with almsfood by me.

He became enraged and said, "As long as nothing is given to the brahmins, or as long as the honoring of kinsmen is not performed, how could you have given the first portion of the meal to that shaven-headed little ascetic?"
Filled with indignation, he said:
"Why does that shaven-headed little ascetic not eat husks?
Through the ripening of that karma, he now eats husks.
The thought occurred to me: "I shall first seek my son's consent;
he will surely feel great joy.
Then I spoke to him.
"Son, rejoice! I have provided the noble Mahākātyāyana with almsfood.

He became enraged and said, "As long as nothing is given to the brahmins, or as long as the honoring of kinsmen is not performed by you, why have you given the first portion of alms to that shaven-headed little ascetic?
And he, filled with indignation, spoke further.
"Why does that shaven-headed, wretched ascetic not eat this iron ball? [The Buddha replied: "It is as a result of the ripening of his own karma that he eats this iron ball.
When the night of the constellations has arrived, my kinsmen send me food offerings."
"I entrust those [gifts] to my daughter-in-law;
having eaten the choice delicacies, she serves me the coarse ones.
I shall send word to those kinsmen."
"Why indeed do you send such coarse refreshments as if during a famine?
They replied to me:
"We do not send coarse refreshments; rather, we send only excellent refreshments."
I said to my daughter-in-law:
"Daughter-in-law, do not eat the choice delicacies yourself and then serve us coarse food.
She replied: [as follows].
"Why does she not eat her own flesh, since it is my food offerings that I am eating?
It is as a result of the ripening of that karma that she eats her own flesh.
When the night of the constellations has arrived, I give exquisite food offerings into the hand of a young girl and send them to my kinsmen.
That girl, having eaten those choice delicacies on the way, served them inferior ones;
they sent word to me, saying:
"Why do you send us such inferior delicacies, as if it were a time of famine?"
"I am sending them word:
'I do not send coarse refreshments; rather, I send only excellent ones.
Thus I spoke to the young women.
"Daughter, do not eat the choice delicacies yourself and then offer them those coarse ones!
She replied,
"Why would she not eat pus and blood who eats your delicacies?"
"Through the ripening of that karma, she eats this pus and blood.
The thought arose in me:
'I shall take rebirth there, where I may see these beings each experiencing their own respective fruits of karma.'"

“Venerable Śroṇa, when I had served the noble Mahākātyāyana with alms-food, I was destined to be reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; however, having made a false aspiration, I have become a preta of great supernatural power.
Śroṇa, you will go to the village of Vāsava; there my daughter works as a courtesan.”
She should be told by you:
"I have seen your father, mother, brother, brother's wife, and servant;
they say this."
"The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this sinful, unrighteous act!
Sister, you say, 'The people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful and will not believe you.'"

"Śroṇa, if he does not believe you, you should say to him: 'In your ancestral dwelling, there are four iron chests filled with gold, and in their midst is a golden staff and water-pot. They will say: "Take these out and satisfy yourself with perfect happiness; from time to time provide alms-food for the noble Mahākātyāyana, and in our name, dedicate the merit. "
"Perhaps this karma might reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total termination.
He made this vow to her.
Thus, as he wandered, twelve years passed by.
He was told by her:
"Śroṇa, will you go to Vāsavagrāma?
"Sister, I shall go."
He ascended that very celestial palace.
She gave this command to those same hungry ghosts:
"Sirs, go, place Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa while he is still asleep in his father’s park in the village of Vāsava, and then return."
He was established by them in the ancestral park at Vāsavagrāmaka.
Upon waking, he saw bells, parasols, and fans, as well as inscribed letters:
"If Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa is still alive, may he come quickly, may he come swiftly; [if] deceased and passed away, [may he attain] a distinguished state from his place of rebirth to another state."
He reflected:
"If my parents have already taken me to be dead, why should I enter the house again? I shall go into the presence of the Venerable Mahākātyāyana and go forth.
Then Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa approached the place where the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was.
The venerable Mahākātyāyana saw Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa from afar;
having seen him, he spoke thus to Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa:
"Come, Śroṇa! Welcome to you. You have seen, Śroṇa, this world and the world beyond."

He said, "I have seen it, venerable Mahākātyāyana. Venerable Mahākātyāyana, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I lead the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."
The noble one said to him, "Śroṇa, first fulfill that previous promise; deliver the messages exactly as you received them.
He then approached that butcher.
"O gentle-faced one, I have seen your father;
he says: 'The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this evil, unrighteous practice.'"
"O man, today it has been twelve years since my father passed away. Has anyone been seen returning from the world beyond?"
"O gentle-faced one, here I am come. He does not believe me.
"Gentle-faced one, if you do not believe, your father says: beneath the place where the sword was buried, there stands a jar full of gold."
"Having extracted yourself from this, satisfy yourself with perfect happiness; provide for the noble Mahākātyāyana with almsfood from time to time, and dedicate the merit in our names.
In this way, perhaps this karma may reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total termination.
He reflected:
"Never before have I heard such a thing; if it should come to pass, all of this will be true.
He went there and dug, and as everything was exactly so, he believed it.
Thereafter, he approached the adulterer;
having approached him, he said:
"Good sir, I have seen your father."
He said, "The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this evil, unrighteous dharma.
He replied:
"O man, today twelve years have passed since my father died.
Have you seen anyone who, having gone to the other world, has returned?
"Good sir, here I am, having come."
He did not believe it. He said, "Good sir, if you do not believe me, your father, beneath the *agniṣṭoma* altar, buried a jar full of gold."
He said:
"Having extracted that [tooth], satisfy yourself with perfect happiness, and from time to time provide alms-food to the noble Mahākātyāyana; and in our name, dedicate the merit.
In this way, perhaps this karma may reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total termination."
He reflected, "I have never heard this before; I shall see for myself. If it should come to pass, all of this will be true.
He went there and dug, and as soon as he saw that everything was exactly as described, he believed it.
He then approached the courtesan.
Having approached, he said:
"Sister, I have seen your mother, father, brother's wife, and servant girl.
They replied: [They say...]
"The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable; desist from this evil, unrighteous act! She said, "O man, today it has been twelve years since my parents passed away."
"Have you seen anyone who, having gone to the next world, has returned? He replied, "I am that very person who has come back."
She did not believe him. He said,
"Sister, if you do not believe me, there are four iron caskets filled with gold remaining in your ancestral father's dwelling."
And in the middle [of the treasure] was a golden staff and water-pot.
They said:
"Having taken that out, satisfy yourself with perfect happiness, and from time to time provide alms-food to the noble Mahākātyāyana; and in our names, dedicate the merit."
"Perhaps this karma will reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total consumption.
She reflected:
"I have never heard such a thing before; I shall see for myself. If it is to come true, then all of this will be real."
She went and dug, and everything was exactly as she had been told; thus it was firmly believed.
Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa reflected:
"This whole world believes in gold, but no one follows me out of faith."
He revealed himself;
in his childhood, his teeth had been bound with gold.
She recognized him.
"Could it be that the noble Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa is thinking of me?
Thus she thought; having gone, she informed his parents.
"Mother, Father, Koṭīkarṇa has arrived!
Thus it was announced to them by many people;
yet they did not go out of faith in anyone.
They said,
"Daughter, you too are mocking us," until he himself had gone.
Standing at the gateway, he made the sound of clearing his throat;
it was the voice of Hiraṇyasvara, and he was recognized by them through that voice.
Embracing them around the neck, they began to weep;
by their tears, the drums burst,
and they began to see.
He said, "Mother and father, give me your permission; out of faith, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless state.
They both replied:
"O sons, weeping out of grief for you, we have become blind; now that you yourself have come, we have regained our sight. As long as we both live, we must not go forth into the religious life."
"When we pass away, you shall go forth.

Having heard the Dharma from the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, he realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), and he established his parents in the refuges and the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). He also studied the four Āgamas.
He realized the fruit of once-returning.
He established his mother and father in the truths.
At another time, his mother and father passed away.
Having given that collection of wealth to the poor, the helpless, the wretched, and the beggars, and having made the destitute no longer destitute, he approached the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Mahākātyāyana and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Śroṇa—
Koṭīkarṇa said this to the venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"Venerable Mahākātyāyana, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya,
so that I may practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."
He was ordained by the Venerable Mahākātyāyana; having gone forth, he studied the Mātṛkās and realized the fruit of a non-returner.
In the regions of Aśmāparāntaka, there were few monks, and it was with great difficulty that a group of ten was completed.
Consequently, a novice (śrāmaṇera) was detained for the three-month period.
Now, it is the nature of things that the disciples of the Blessed Buddhas have two assemblies.
There are those who [assemble] on the full moon of Āṣāḍhī, the commencement of the rainy season, and those who [assemble] on the full moon of Kārttikī.

Among them, those who assemble on the full moon of Āṣāḍhī, the commencement of the rainy season, take up and master various scriptural recitations, yogic practices, and mental applications, and then enter the rains retreat in various villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
Those who assemble on the full moon day of Kārttika announce what they have attained and inquire further about what follows;
it is exactly the same for the great śrāvakas as well.

Then those monks who were the co-residents and pupils of the venerable Mahākātyāyana, having mastered and fully grasped various specific instructions, yogic practices, and mental attentions, entered the rains retreat in various villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
At the conclusion of those three months of the rainy season, having prepared their robes and finished making them ready, they took up their bowls and outer robes.
They approached the venerable Mahākātyāyana;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Mahākātyāyana and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, they reported what they had understood and asked further questions.
A group of ten was complete;
he was ordained by that [group],
and by him the Tripiṭaka was studied.

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship. He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, having shattered the eggshell of ignorance, attained the clear knowledges, superknowledges, and analytical insights, and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra.
Then, the venerable Mahākātyāyana’s co-residents and disciples, having attended upon the venerable Mahākātyāyana for as long as they were with him, said this to the venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"We have seen our preceptor, and we have attended upon him."
"Let us go; we shall attend upon the Blessed One.
"Child, do so.
For the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are indeed to be attended upon."
Now at that time, Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa was seated and present in that very assembly.

Then the Venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, extending his joined palms toward the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, bowed down to the Venerable one.
He said this to Mahākātyāyana:
"By the power of my preceptor, I have seen that Blessed One by means of his Dharma-body, but not by means of his form-body."
"I am going, Preceptor; I shall see that Blessed One even with my physical body.
He said, "Do so, dear child."
"Indeed, dear son, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are difficult to behold, just like the flower of the udumbara tree.
In our name, bow your head at the feet of the Blessed One, and inquire after his freedom from illness, his vigor, and his dwelling in comfort; then ask him five questions.
Venerable Sir, in the Aśmāparāntaka regions, there are few monks, and it is with great difficulty that a group of ten is completed."
In that regard, how should we proceed?
The ground is hard and covered with cow-thorns;
in the bordering regions of Aśmāparāntaka, such is the manner of the rugs and coverlets, namely: the skin of a goat, the skin of an ox, the skin of a deer, and the skin of a sheep.

In other regions, such bedding and coverlets as these exist— namely, eraka, meraka, janduraka, and manduraka. In the very same way, in the Aśmāparāntaka regions, there are such bedding and coverlets as these—
namely, goat-skins, and so forth as previously described.
People who purify themselves with water have the practice of bathing.
A monk sends robes for another monk;
they fall from here but have not yet reached there.
"To whom do these natural [powers] belong?
The Venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa consented to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana by remaining silent.
Then, when that very night had passed, in the forenoon, the Venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered the village of Vāsava for alms.
Eventually, having reached Śrāvastī in due course,
the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa set aside his bowl and robe, washed his feet, and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage, he sat down to one side.

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and prepare a couch in a single dwelling for both the Tathāgata and Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa. "So be it, Venerable Sir," replied the venerable Ānanda. Having prepared [the couch] for both the Tathāgata and Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, a couch has been prepared for the Tathāgata and for Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa in a single dwelling; may the Blessed One do as he deems timely.
Then the Blessed One went to the dwelling of Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, and having entered the dwelling, he sat down.
Having established mindfulness before him,

the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa likewise washed his feet outside the monastery, entered the monastery, sat down, and having crossed his legs and set his body erect, he established mindfulness before him.
During that very night, the Blessed One and the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa passed the time in noble silence.
Then, at the break of dawn, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa:
"May the Dharma, Śroṇa, which has been realized by me through my own direct knowledge and fully awakened to, be proclaimed by you."

Then the Venerable Śroṇa, having been granted leave by the Blessed One, recited aloud in detail with a clear voice the Udānas, the Pārāyaṇa, the Satyadṛṣṭas, the Śailagāthās, the Munigāthās, the Sthaviragāthās, the Sthavirīgāthās, and the Arthavargīya sūtras from the Aśmāparāntaka collection of Svaraguptika.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa had finished his discourse, said this to the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa:
"Excellent, excellent, Śroṇa! The Dharma you have spoken is sweet and sublime—precisely that which I myself, having realized it through direct knowledge and attained awakening, have proclaimed.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa:

Thinking, "This is my time to fulfill the word of the Blessed One, my preceptor," he rose from his seat and, having bowed down to the Blessed One, spoke as follows: "Venerable sir, in the country of the Aśmāparāntakas, in the village of Vāsavagrāmaka, dwells the venerable Mahākātyāyana, who is my preceptor."

He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and inquired after his freedom from illness, his ease of movement, and his state of well-being, up to his dwelling in comfort; he then asked five questions, which should be recited in detail.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa:
"Śroṇa, it is not the right time for you to have your question answered.
A question should be asked in the midst of the Saṃgha;
there will be the proper time for answering your question."
Then the Blessed One, having risen early in the morning, sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"In the country of the Aśmāparāntakas, at Vāsavagrāmaka, the venerable Mahākātyāyana resides; he is my preceptor.

He bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One and inquires after his health, asking whether he is free from affliction and living in comfort. Furthermore, he reports five questions in detail, just as they were previously stated, ending with: 'To whom do these things belong by way of forfeiture?'"
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize full ordination in border regions by a group consisting of a fifth member who is an expert in the Vinaya."
One should always bathe.
Sandals made of a single leaf of *palāśa* should be worn, not those of two layers or three layers.
If they become subject to wear and tear, they should be worn after attaching a heel-strap.
If they are subject to decay, they should be held with a support or worn with a leather strap.
When a monk sends robes for a monk, if they fall from here and have not yet reached there, they do not become subject to forfeiture for anyone. (MSV IV 190)
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir,
regarding what was said by the Blessed One— that in the border regions, ordination may be performed by a group consisting of a master of the Vinaya as the fifth member—
what is the interior region and what is the border region?"
To the east, Upāli, is the city named Puṇḍravardhana; to the east of that is the forest named Puṇḍrakakṣa.
That is the interior.
Beyond that is the borderland.
To the south is a city named Śarāvatī;
beyond that is the river named Śarāvatī.
That is the interior;
beyond that is the borderland.
To the west are the two Brahmin villages of Sthūṇa and Upasthūṇaka.
That is the interior;
beyond that is the borderland;
to the north is Mount Uśīra.
That is the interior;
beyond that is the borderland.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.

"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, as the ripening of which karma he was born into a family that was wealthy, of great fortune, and of great possessions; with a jeweled earring set with gems fastened upon his ear, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and, through the abandonment of all afflictions, realized arhatship?"
The Blessed One said:
"In the past, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there arose in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, a Blessed One and Teacher named Kāśyapa.
At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there were two people, a husband and wife."
In the presence of Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, they both undertook the going for refuge and the precepts of training.
When Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, having completed the entire work of a Buddha, entered the realm of nirvana without remainder of substrate...

When he had passed into parinirvāṇa, King Kṛkī had a stūpa made of the four precious substances constructed, one yojana in circumference and half a yojana in height. For the purpose of repairing any cracks or damage there, the taxes and revenues that were collected at the eastern city gate were assigned to that stūpa. When King Kṛkī died, his son named Sujāta was established in his own kingdom.
The ministers presented only a small amount of tax revenue to him.
The king asked,
"For what reason have you presented such a small amount of tax revenue to us?"
"Do taxes and revenues arise in our realm?
They replied,
"Your Majesty, from where would taxes and revenues arise?"

"O King, those taxes and revenues that were previously assigned at the eastern gate for the restoration of the stūpa’s broken and dilapidated parts have been designated by the elder king. If Your Majesty permits, we shall abolish those taxes and revenues.
He replied:
"Gentlemen, whatever was done by my father was indeed done by Brahmā.
They reflected:
"If Your Majesty permits, we shall act in such a way that those taxes and revenues will not arise of their own accord."
They closed that gate and established it;
no longer did taxes or tributes arise.
And on that stūpa, cracks appeared.
Those two, husband and wife, having grown old, remained right there performing maintenance work on the stūpa.
And from the northern region, a caravan leader, having taken his merchandise, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
He saw that stūpa, which had become cracked and broken;
having seen it, he asked,
"Mother, Father, whose stūpa is this?"
The two of them said:
"Of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa;
by whom was it caused to be made?"
By King Kṛkin;
nothing was provided by that king for the repair of what was broken or decayed in this stūpa.
The two of them said:
The taxes and revenues that were previously assigned at the eastern city gate have now been dedicated toward the restoration of this stūpa’s broken and dilapidated parts.
King Kṛkī has passed away;
his son, named Sujāta, has been established in his own kingdom.
Because of that, those taxes and revenues were cut off;
because of that, cracks and fissures appeared in this stūpa.
He had a jewel-earring fastened upon his ear.
Having brought it down, she gave it to them,
saying, "Mother and Father, with this jeweled earring, perform repairs on the cracks and fissures of this stūpa until I return after having disposed of my merchandise;
thereafter, I shall give you more."

Having sold it to them, they carried out the restoration of that stūpa’s broken and dilapidated parts and further improved it. Then, at another time, that caravan leader returned after having disposed of his merchandise.
He saw him at the stūpa, his appearance beyond compare; having seen him, he became even more deeply inspired with faith. Having conceived this faith, he asked:
"Mother, father, has nothing been set aside by you as a reserve?
They replied, "Son, nothing has been set aside by us; however, another portion remains outstanding."
Having conceived that faith, he gave whatever remained there as well as other offerings, performed a great worship, and made this aspiration:
"By this root of merit, may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;
and may I become a recipient of such qualities as these."
"May I please such a Teacher as this, and may I never displease him.
What do you think, monks?
That caravan leader was none other than Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa himself.

Because he performed service at the stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa and made a formal aspiration, through the ripening of that karma, he was born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;
and having gone forth in my teaching, by abandoning all afflictions, he has realized arhatship.

"Monks, I have pleased, and not displeased, this Teacher Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, being equal in strength, equal in speed, equal in burden, and having attained the same common status as he. For indeed, monks, the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black;
the ripening of entirely white karmas is entirely white; and that of mixed karmas is mixed."
"Therefore, monks, having abandoned entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The monks said:
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Śroṇakoṭīkarṇa, the ripening of which caused him to see the states of woe in this very life?
The Blessed One said,
"Because he uttered harsh words toward his mother, it was as the ripening of that karma that he saw the states of woe in this very life."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. The Venerable Upananda was the most junior member of the Saṅgha; he received a creaking wooden bedstead in the row of assignments.
He turns about out of fear; thinking,
"It might break," he reflects,
"I am Upananda, and I even long for a couch."
"I shall not bear the name 'Upananda' unless I provide a bed or a couch. Rising early in the morning, he approached King Prasenajit of Kosala. He was addressed by the king as follows:
"Welcome, Venerable Upananda!
Has the Venerable Upananda slept well?
He replied:
"Gillapeṭha, do you not know that just as I prepare an eight-layered bed, so too does Upananda?
I am the youngest member of the Saṃgha, and I have received a creaking couch from my own rank;
thus, I turn over out of fear."
"It will not break," he thought.
"Such an eight-layered bed for the Venerable Upananda is quite permissible; it is very well permissible.
Where was this prohibited? And by whom was it prohibited?
"If it seems appropriate to you, let it be accepted.
Upananda said,
"What business do I have with the Kosala country?"
Having dedicated a monastery, he bestowed it upon him;
by that [act], eight men were assigned to him.
There, four took charge of the bedding and seating, while four took charge of the couches.
Having taken them, they set out through the middle of the street.
They were seen by the brahmins and householders, and having seen them, they asked:
"Where, venerable sirs, will you prepare his royal bed?
Upananda replied,
"In our own home."
"To whom is this bed being taken?
Upananda replied,
"I obtained it."
They reproached him, reviled him,
and spoke against him, saying, "Venerable one, how can the qualities of sensual pleasure trouble this ascetic Upananda?
For he went to the monastery and, having sprinkled and swept the dwelling, applied a fine coating of cow dung."
"Having prepared my bed, I shall sit down.
And the Blessed One arrived at that place;
filled with joy, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, look at what kind of bed mine is!
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, from the very beginning, the foolish man Upananda should be known as a 'guardian'."
The Blessed One reflected:
"Whatever fault there is, it is because monks make use of high beds and large beds.
Therefore, a monk must not sit upon a high bed or a large bed."
If one sits down [on such a seat], one commits an offense of transgression. The Blessed One has said: "A monk must not sit on a high bed or a large couch."
A certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, into his home.
He began to prepare high seats.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda entered.
He saw someone preparing high seats;
he was addressed by him:
"Householder, these seats are not suitable for monks."
"Remove them! He began to remove them,
and the Blessed One arrived there.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are inquisitive and ask questions.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, what is this that you are about to do?"
“Blessed One, this householder is preparing very costly beds and seats.
“Householder, these beds and seats are not suitable for a monk;
remove them.”
This very person is leading him away. Ānanda, restrain the householder! Let them prepare [the meal]; it will not be possible for everyone, Ānanda.
Therefore, I authorize that one may sit on a high seat within a house,
but must not lie down;
however, one must never sit on a high seat in a monastery.
If one lies down on a seat, one commits an offense of transgression.
A certain monk, possessing only the three robes, arrived at Śrāvastī from the Southern Road to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One;
he had a beautiful leather mat.
He was seen there by Upananda, who said to him:
"O alms-collector, give this hide to me; I am one who pays homage to the caityas."
"I am going to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
He said,
"Venerable Upananda, is this proper or improper?"
"I too have come here to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. I thought you were a mendicant who lives on alms;
Venerable Upananda, are you capable or incapable of taking up such a hide as this?"
"Look, Venerable Upananda, because you are incapable of that which I am capable of, I will not give it to you;
I am going. He said:
"Venerable Upānanda, you go to the residence;
I have come here solely to pay homage to the shrine and to prostrate at the feet [of the Buddha].
Do you not know, Upānanda, that you are incapable of procuring such a hide?"
"See, Venerable Upananda, I will not give it to you for that which you are incapable of [performing].
King Prasenajit of Kosala has a cowherd named Baḍra who is a close friend of the Venerable Upananda.
He then approached him.
In the spring season, a variegated and beautifully marked calf was born. She stroked the back of one calf,
and Baḍra said:
"Venerable Upananda, do you desire the milk of this mother?
This is not it."
He said,
"Let this be so;
however, whichever monk has such a hide, let him apply himself to the side of wholesome qualities without much concern."
He said,
"Venerable Upananda, go; it is understood."
He departed.
He gave an order to the cowherd: "Slay this calf, take its hide, and having brought it, present it to the venerable Upananda.
Having slain that calf and taken its hide, he set out.
Out of affection for her calf, that cow followed closely behind, lowing "haṃbha.
Having entered the Jeta Grove, the cow stood at the gate of the Jeta Grove, uttering the sound "haṃbha.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are those who know and those who inquire.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why does this cow stand at the gate of Jetavana?
The venerable Ānanda replied:
“Blessed One, her calf was caused to be killed by the venerable Upananda for the sake of its hide;
therefore, this cow stands at the gate of the Jeta Grove, lowing with cries of distress.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, whatever disadvantage there is in monks wearing leather,
therefore a monk must not wear leather. Those who do wear it become guilty of an offense."
The Blessed One said,
"One must not wear skins.
A certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha.
He began to prepare seats of leather;
however, as before, they would not be available everywhere.
Therefore, one may sit on a leather seat within a house, but one must not lie down upon it.
One must not sit down nor lie down in the monastery;
if one sits down or lies down, one incurs an offense of transgression.
The setting was Rājagṛha. A vehicle was permitted for Pilindavatsa because he was constantly ill.
Thereupon, the group of six monks began to travel by vehicle.
Therefore, one should not travel by vehicle;
that itself is a disadvantage.
Consequently, one should travel by two [persons]: either one who is aged or physically weak from old age, or one who is ill and incapable of exertion.
The monks were wandering through the countryside and went to a river; they were unable to cross it while carrying their bowls and robes.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"A monk must learn how to swim."
The group of six monks was crossing the Ajiravatī river; they were crossing even by wading through the stream.
When they had finished crossing and arrived, [the nuns said:
"Sisters, we will ferry you across; do so."
With those [hands], they touched their major and minor limbs.
"Come back again!
they said. They replied:
"Those regions which were not even touched by our master have been touched by you.
They reproached him, reviled him, and spoke against him.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, whatever disadvantage there is in touching a woman, therefore a monk must not touch a woman.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
Women should not be touched;
the people of the city are fond of pleasure gardens.
While they were in the park, a certain woman went down to the river for the sake of water;
she became thirsty,
and a man walked along looking at her.
He saw a monk;
the noble one saw a certain woman floating;
he saw her and thought, "She is floating."
"Standing and looking for water throughout the day, her life-force is thus exhausted. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"She must be rescued.
Others said, "Let her go;
they have become exceedingly powerful."
Some are to be released;
others become motionless.
Having made them into a heap of girl-bodies, they place them upside down, cast them away, and depart.
They were being devoured by jackals;
they should not leave them behind and go away.
They became attached.
One should remain in a secluded place.
Those monks who are reciters should engage in recitation;
those who are meditators should apply themselves to mental attention.
There will be a lack of food;
one should travel along with those who are cowherds or shepherds there.
The group of six crosses by means of a cow's tail.
There was a certain householder who had cows;
he continued to milk them until their milk had completely disappeared.
He asked the cowherd,
"Why is there no milk today?
They replied:
By the noble ones of the group-of-six, as before;
he reproaches, reviles, and censures [them].
Therefore, a monk must not cross by holding onto a cow's tail.
The Blessed One said:
"One should not cross by means of a cow's tail.
Consequently, the monks encountered difficulty in crossing a river.
They did not wish to cross by means of an elephant's tail. The Blessed One said: "One should cross by means of the tails of five young elephants."
[It is not like crossing] with a well-bred elephant, a well-bred horse, a bull, a buffalo, or a yak;
rather, one must cross by means of a raft.
The Blessed One has said: "One must cross by means of a raft."
The group of six monks made various variegated paintings of lotus-patterned cloth depicting men and women in states of sexual union.
When they were seen by brahmins and householders, the latter asked, "Sirs, what is this?"
They said,
"We have been permitted by the Blessed One, the Seer.
They then reproached them.
"Noble one, you possess the sensual pleasures of a recluse.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Monks must not wear rugs that are variegated or multicolored and as large as a lotus, nor should they wear rugs used by men and women who have committed sexual misconduct.
Rather, there are only two types of rugs permitted: the saffron-colored one and the *tāraṇika*.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada had a circular pavilion constructed for the hearing of the Dharma,
[using] wooden sandals.
The monks arrived;
by them, that paved floor was made scarred and torn by their wooden sandals.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having risen very early, came to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
He saw him;
having seen him, he said:
"Venerable ones, has King Prasenajit arrived here for the night with a fourfold army?"
They said,
"It was not the king, but rather the monks who came wearing wooden sandals;
by them this has been destroyed."
He was censured.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One reflected:
"Monks, whatever disadvantage there is in monks wearing wooden sandals, therefore a monk must not wear wooden sandals.
It was said by the Blessed One: 'A monk must not wear wooden sandals.'"
The monks entered private houses,
and their sandals became soaked with mud.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"A monk should wear wooden sandals within a house.
Pure brahmins and householders offer wooden sandals to the monks in the Saṅgha."
The monks did not accept it.
They said,
"Noble one, when the Blessed One had not yet appeared in the world, at that time the heretics were the ones worthy of offerings."
The Blessed One said:
"It should be accepted.
Having accepted it, it should be thrown into a communal latrine or a urinal."
The summary verse: Bamboo leaves, Śroṇa, and what is permitted for protection;
the crosswise-fastened, the former, the heel, and the fold.
The Blessed One said,
"Wooden sandals must not be worn. They, however, wore sandals made of bamboo leaves.
That itself is the disadvantage.
The Blessed One said:
"One must not wear sandals made of bamboo leaves."
They wear sandals made of muñja grass;
that is indeed a disadvantage.
The Blessed One said:
One should not wear sandals made of muñja grass.
They wore sandals made of rope;
that very same disadvantage [remained].
The Blessed One said:
"Straw sandals must not be worn.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
"It was said that corded sandals should not be worn. However, the monks suffered from wind-disorders and blood disorders; by means of pouring water over them, their leather sandals became damp.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"He who suffers from wind-blood disorder (vātaśoṇita) should wear cord sandals.
When Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa had gone forth, the members of the group-of-six (ṣaḍvargika) saw that on the soles of his feet there were golden-colored hairs, four finger-breadths in length.
Seeing them, they said, "This is merely a lump of fresh butter; what will he do by going forth in a teaching that is so difficult to practice?
He heard this.
Having heard this, pride arose in him;
he approached the Venerable Ānanda,
and having approached, he questioned the Venerable Ānanda.

"Venerable Ānanda, what is this 'one-pointed concentration' spoken of by the Blessed One? It is the attainment through walking meditation, friend Śroṇa. Having said this, he went to the Śītavana cemetery and established himself upon a walking path.
As he was walking, his gold-colored body hairs, each four finger-breadths in length, fell away;
thereafter the skin, and thereafter the blood.
As long as he went from one end of the walkway to the other, [the same occurred] for him at one [end].
Crows were drinking blood at the head of the walking path, and likewise at the second one.

It is indeed the natural law that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while living, staying, enduring, and maintaining themselves, go on river-walks from time to time; in detail, for this purpose, the Buddha, the Blessed One, went on a walk through the monastery grounds.
Wandering toward the monastery where the venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa resided, the Blessed One arrived there.
The Blessed One beheld the walking-path of Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa.
And having seen this, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—who know and yet inquire—asked.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the Venerable Ānanda about the walking path of the monk Ekāntaghaṭaka:
"Venerable sir, whose [path] is it? "It is that of Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa."
"Therefore, Ānanda, I authorize Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa to wear sandals with a single layer of leather, neither double-layered nor triple-layered.
If they become worn out, they should be worn after attaching a heel-protector.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa.
Having approached Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, he said this to him:
"Venerable Śroṇa, you should know that the Teacher has permitted you sandals with a single layer of leather, not double-layered," and so forth.
"Venerable Ānanda, is this for the entire Saṅgha, or for me alone?"
"It is for you alone, Venerable Ānanda; the Teacher’s command is not to be transgressed. If I were to retain it, my fellow practitioners might, on that account, speak against me."

There, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa attained a great deal [of merit] through his going forth— he who, having abandoned the city of Campā, which was unique to him, and an army of seven elephants, went forth, yet now is attached to even a mere pair of sandals.
However, if the Blessed One...
"Having assembled, let the entire Saṃgha grant its permission; thus shall I maintain [this rule].
The Venerable Ānanda reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Śroṇa Koṭiviṃśa, I authorize that upon his arrival, sandals with a single layer of leather shall be worn by the entire Saṅgha, and not those with two layers," and so forth.
Now, a certain elderly monk was walking back and forth in front of the Blessed One wearing sandals.
Then the Blessed One said this to that monk:
"Go away, monk; do not stand before me.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, when a teacher is defiled by the worldly pleasures of all the world, even the disciples of that teacher do not very quickly fall into a state of transgression."
"How much less, then, do I dwell detached from all worldly pleasures?
The Blessed One reflected:
"Whatever fault there is in monks wearing sandals, therefore a monk must not wear sandals."
A certain Śobhita had gone forth as a monk;
his water-vessel was broken.
Having washed his feet at the foot-washing stand, he [washed] his face with water.
Having filled it with water, he set out with the gait of a peacock.
He was seen by the group of six monks, who said:
"Venerable ones, a monk is dancing without musical instruments; play some music! they said, and so they began to play mouth-instruments.
They were rebuked by the monks: "Why do you act with such levity?
They replied:
"What is the frivolity here?
Do you not see, monks, that monk dancing without musical instruments?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers who ask; knowing, they ask.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked that monk: "With what intention, monk, was this done?
"For the sake of protecting the bedding and seating, Venerable Sir."
There is no offense for this monk when he acts solely for the purpose of protecting his bedding and seating.
Therefore, I authorize that sandals made of a single layer of palāśa leaves should be worn for the purpose of protecting one's bedding and seating.
It should not have two layers, nor three layers.
If it is subject to decay, it should be kept by inserting a bolt.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"One should wear sandals made of a single leaf.
Now, a certain householder was devoted to a certain alms-collecting monk.
Being without shoes, he entered Śrāvastī for alms. That householder saw him without shoes,
and having seen him, he said:
"The Noble One has no sandals. Come, let us go to the cobbler; I shall have him give you some."
He went to the presence of a shoemaker and said to him,
"Please give a pair of sandals to the noble one," and having spoken thus, he departed.
At that time, sandals with a single layer of leather were being made for both the monks and those who had passed away.
That monk approached the cobbler again and again,
but he would not give them to him.
At another time, that householder again saw the monk without sandals;
having seen him, he said,
"Noble one, those sandals were not given to you by that craftsman."
"Householder, have you not heard that an artisan who speaks the truth is rare?
Though I approached you again and again, you did not grant me [the payment].
He said:"
"Noble one, come; let us go home.
Having led him home, he satisfied him with excellent food and gave him a multi-layered sandal.
The monk said:
"Householder, it has not been permitted by the Blessed One.
He said, "Noble one, go; having folded it into a single layer, you shall wear it."
Having taken it, he went to the monastery.
Carrying both that [stone] and a small knife, he went to the foot of a tree and began to pry it up.
At that moment, the Blessed One arrived at that place.
"O Bhikṣu, what is to be done?
The Blessed One has prohibited multi-layered sandals, yet I have obtained only a multi-layered one; I shall wear it after making it single-layered."
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:

"Alas, these faithful householders will give multi-layered sandals to the disciples. Therefore, I authorize that multi-layered sandals, having been made free from household characteristics, should be worn. The Venerable Upāli asked [the Buddha] as follows.
"Venerable sir, it was said by the Blessed One that a multi-layered sandal should be made by those who have renounced the life of a householder and worn.
To what extent, venerable sir, is something said to have been 'renounced by a householder'?
At minimum, Upāli, it is when seven or eight layers have been removed."
The setting was Vaiśālī.
At that time, in Vaiśālī, sandals of this kind were being made:
namely, those that made a "hini-hinā" sound and a "kiṇi-kiṇā" sound, shaped like the horns of rams, with soles of bodhi-tree bark, variegated and beautifully decorated, and worth five kārṣāpaṇas.

The group of six monks saw [a man] covering his sandals; they tore open his heels and big toes with their thumbs, loosened them at the neck, and took them, saying, "This gift is for the adornment of your mind.
A report spread throughout the vicinity:
"The venerable ones are taking away sandals of such a kind!"
A son-in-law arrived with a certain young woman;
she gave him her sandals and said, "Noble sir, they take away sandals."
"You must be heedful so that you do not cause [the food] to be taken away.
A *piṇḍapātika* (alms-collector) entered for alms;
he saw him having entered into one house.
He too entered that very place;
having emerged from that house, he entered another house,
and the alms-collector also entered that same place.
He said,
"Noble one, for what purpose have you followed closely behind me?
Do you wish to take away my sandals?"
"O gentle-faced one, I am not taking away your sandals; rather, I am entering for alms.
He replied, "Noble sir, whether you take them or not, the report has already spread throughout your neighborhood that 'the noble ones are stealing sandals.'"
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"Whatever disadvantage there may be, monks, when they wear such sandals as these—'hinihini' and so forth, in detail."
Therefore, a monk must not wear sandals of this kind, such as those that make a *hinihinikā* sound; [this is] the full detail.
If a monk wears sandals of this kind, he commits an offense of transgression.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, wounds had been caused on the backs of the monks' feet by their sandals. When the brahmins and householders saw them,
they asked, "By whom have these wounds been inflicted upon you?"
"Why do you not wear sandals with the straps fastened horizontally?
This has not been permitted by the Blessed One."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"A horizontal bandage should be worn."
On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa at Rājagṛha,
as those who were ascending the mountain, their big toes became wounded;
these were seen by the brahmins and householders.
"By whom were your big toes wounded as you were ascending Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain?
You should not wear sandals."
"It was not authorized by the Blessed One.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
It should be worn.
For those who descend right there, their heels become wounded.
[The rule] should be observed as before, up until it is worn.
The summary verse:
*Nālāmbuja*, *muṇḍapūla*, and *pūla* among the Himalayas;
bear-skin is permitted, as well as a needle, a knife, and a binding-thong.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
The feet of the monks were pierced by new grass.
The brahmins and householders said:
"By what have your feet been pierced with thorns? By fresh grass.
Why do you not wear lotus stalks?"
"It was not authorized by the Blessed One.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
Lotus stalks are to be carried;
likewise, when the grass is old, bundles of *muṇḍa* grass are to be carried;

When the foolish man Virūḍhaka had slaughtered the Śākyans of Kapilavastu, some went to the Northern Region and others entered as far as Naivāla.
Merchants from Śrāvastī had gone to Naivāla,
and they questioned those merchants.
"Arya Ānanda, who is so affectionate toward his kinsmen, does not look after us.
When this was reported to him by them,
he did not even enter.
His feet were cracked by the cold.
He was asked by the monks,
"For what reason have your feet now become like this?"
"By means of snow?
What do those relatives of yours do?
They wear felt."
"Why do you not wear it?
"It has not been authorized by the Blessed One.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In the Himalayan regions, felt rugs (pūla) should be worn.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:

"Venerable One, as it was said by the Blessed One that 'in the Himalayan regions, felt rugs (pūla) should be worn,' which are those Himalayan regions? They are those places where a water vessel freezes."
A hunter had developed faith in a certain monk;
he possessed a bear skin and offered it to that monk.
He did not take it,
and the Blessed One arrived at that place;
for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers who inquire.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why is this hunter following closely behind that monk?"
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, faith in a hunter is difficult to find."
If he obtains even a hundred thousand [pieces of meat], he slaughters them all.
Therefore, if a hunter offers a bear’s skin,
it should be accepted.
Having taken it, it should be placed at the door of the fragrant chamber or at the foot of the bed;
all bear skin is beneficial for the eyes and brings well-being.

He who possesses skill should, standing in a secluded place, tie it together.
He said,
"I have been authorized by the Blessed One."
"For tying; therein there is need for a needle, a small blade, and a binding cord.
